title: Rosé styles
subtitle: Pink wine, three ways
objectives: Explain how rosé gets its colour
Describe the three ways to make rosé
Explain why blending red and white is rare

steps.title: Pink from the skins
steps.body: Rosé is made from black grapes whose juice touches the skins only briefly, usually from 2 to 20 hours. That's enough for a little colour and fruit, but very little tannin. Most rosé is dry, like those of Provence, though some, like White Zinfandel, are sweet.
steps.highlight: Rosé: black grapes, short skin contact

steps.title: Three methods
steps.body: Direct pressing squeezes black grapes gently, giving the palest rosés. Short maceration leaves the juice on the skins for some hours, then runs it off to ferment like a white. Saignée, French for bleeding, draws juice off a red wine tank early; the rosé is a by-product and the remaining red becomes more concentrated.

steps.prompt: Match each rosé method to how it works.
steps.explanation: All three methods limit skin contact. Provence is the region most associated with pale, dry rosé.

steps.body: Mixing red and white wine to make rosé is banned for most European wines. Rosé Champagne is the famous exception, where a little red wine is often blended in.

steps.prompt: In saignée, the main goal of the producer is often the red wine, not the rosé.
steps.explanation: Yes. Bleeding off some juice leaves a higher ratio of skins to juice in the tank, so the red becomes deeper. The rosé is a useful by-product.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rosé gets its colour from a short contact with black grape skins
It is made by direct press, short maceration or saignée
Blending red and white is banned for most European rosé, except Champagne
